syllabusTopics: Limits and continuity: limits of a function, indeterminate forms, algebraic properties of limits (without proof), basic theorems on limits of algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs of discontinuous function
Derivatives: derivative of a function, derivatives of algebraic, trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions by definition (simple forms)
Rules of differentiation; derivatives of parametric and implicit functions; higher order derivatives
Geometric interpretation of derivative; monotonicity of a function, interval of monotonicity, extreme values of a function, concavity, points of inflection
Anti-derivatives: integration using basic integrals, integration by substitution and by parts methods
The definite integral; the definite integral as an area under the given curve; area between two curves

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Substituting the point and stopping — the limit asks what the function APPROACHES, not what it equals there.  ·  Concluding the limit exists because both sides are 'big' — they must be the SAME FINITE number; $0/0$ or $-\infty/+\infty$ is a jump.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The exclusion of $x=a$ in the epsilon-delta definition is the key subtlety: it is what makes a limit independent of the function's value at the point.  ·  $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$ holds only in radians; in degrees the value is $\frac{\pi}{180}$.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The layered race*** - (e^{2x}-1-2x)/x^2: the 2x cancels the exponential's first order, leaving the second-order star 1/2 - diagnosis in layers, not one glance.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Writing $\lim = \infty$ as a result — a divergent limit says the function is unbounded, not that it reached a value.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: State and interpret the epsilon-delta definition.  ·  Evaluate limits using factorisation, conjugates and standard trigonometric limits.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Read the form, take the table's row, execute; stars before L'Hopital, ladder before division.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (e^{2x} − 1 − 2x)/x².** — **Layered diagnosis:** e^{2x} − 1 ~ 2x (first order) — so the numerator's first-order part 2x cancels it exactly, and the contest moves to **second order**. **Second-order star:** (eᵘ − 1 − u)/u² → **1/2** as u → 0 (the exponential's parabolic correction).…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} [x²·sin(1/x)]/sin x.** — **Two theorems chained:** numerator — the damped oscillator x²sin(1/x) → **0** by squeeze (amplitude x² vanishes); denominator — sin x ~ **x** by the first-order star. **Assemble:** the expression = [x²sin(1/x)/x]·[x/sin x] → [x·sin(1/x)]·[1] → **0** by squeeze (amplitude x).…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: One confirming cross-check per answer - star vs factor, ladder vs L'Hopital.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Route table: substitution (continuity), 0/0 (factor/conjugate/steer/L'Hopital), c/0 (wall signs), damped oscillator (squeeze), joints (two-sided audit), infinity (degrees/ladder), power forms (log bridge). Selection is the exam skill - cheapest working route wins.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Every limits problem in the syllabus falls to one row of the route table.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (5m): Evaluate lim_{x→π/2⁻} tan x and lim_{x→π/2⁺} tan x, and classify the discontinuity of tan at π/2.** — **Left side:** cos x → 0⁺ (x below π/2), sin x → 1 ⟹ tan x = sin/cos → **+∞**. **Right side:** cos x → 0⁻ ⟹ → **−∞**.…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (x + sin x)/x, and explain why L'Hôpital's rule cannot certify it.** — **Route — split legally:** (x + sin x)/x = 1 + sin x/x → 1 + 0 = **1** (the star sin x/x → 0 at infinity by squeeze: |sin x/x| ≤ 1/x → 0).…

rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Capstone Limits Drill This canonical is the **capstone limits drill**: mixed problems spanning the whole limits toolkit — substitution, transformation, stars, squeeze, walls, and infinity — in exam format. It mirrors the parent limit-system canonical; the drill's discipline is route selection under time pressure.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror — The Route Table | Symptom | Route | |---|---| | Substitution works | cite continuity, evaluate | | 0/0 | factor / conjugate / steer / L'Hôpital | | c/0 | wall: signs by side | | Oscillator damped | squeeze | | Piecewise joint | LHL, RHL, compare | | ∞ forms | degrees, ladder, dominant division | | 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰ | log bridge |  ·  ## 3. Deep Conceptual — Route Selection as the Exam Skill - Every limits problem has **several working routes and one cheapest**: the coefficient ratio beats the L'Hôpital passes; the ladder beats the dominant division; the squeeze beats any transformation of an oscillator. Capstone drills train the *selection*, which is where exam time is won.…

rows.text: NEB-style practice beyond the verified PYQs recorded on the parent canonicals.  ·  When a route stalls, re-diagnose - persistence with a stalled route is the only failure.  ·  Evaluate lim_{x→0} (e^{2x} − 1 − 2x)/x².

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Evaluate lim_{x→0} x²·sin(1/x)/sin x.  ·  Evaluate lim_{x→π/2⁻} tan x and classify the discontinuity.  ·  Locate vertical and horizontal asymptotes from limits.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 4. Deep Conceptual — Mixed Problems Test Architecture, Not Memory - A capstone item like (e^{2x} − 1 − 2x)/x² requires *layered* diagnosis: the 2x term cancels the exponential's first order, so the contest is at second order — the (eᵘ − 1 − u)/u² → 1/2 refinement.…  ·  ## 5. Worked Example Types - **Type A — layered 0/0:** first-order cancellation exposes second-order stars. - **Type B — squeeze + star chains:** damped oscillator over a vanishing denominator. - **Type C — wall + classification:** c/0 with side signs and the continuity verdict.…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **"Always L'Hôpital":** the stars are cheaper and always legal where they apply. **"The squeeze needs equal rails":** it needs rails converging to the *same* value — boundedness alone proves nothing.
